13824-the-national-preacher-vol-2-no-7-d:
Austin Dickinson edited The National Preacher as a monthly of original sermons. This December 1827 number, volume two, number seven, prints sermons by Dr. Leland and Mr. Baldwin. Postage rates on the cover show how the magazine travelled by mail across the young republic. An appeal to clergy proposes a new periodical of pastoral sketches.

The sermons stress faith, duty, and the danger of lowering divine truth to human taste. Preachers warn against moulding doctrine to suit unholy inclinations. The language is earnest and direct, aimed at ministers and devout readers. The issue captures American evangelical preaching before the Civil War. It also shows early religious publishing in action.
21943-peter-schlemihl:
A man sells his shadow to a stranger in Peter Schlemihl, Adelbert von Chamisso's famous German tale, Englished here by Sir John Bowring in 1861. George Cruikshank's plates show Schlemihl giving his shadow away, the bargain that ruins and remakes him. The translator's notice tells how Adelung promised him at Petersburg: read it, and you will translate it. He did, with only trifling changes.

Bowring calls the story a moral one and leaves its lessons to the reader's own eye. Chamisso, a French-born German poet and botanist, wrote the tale in a few weeks of 1813. It became a European classic, and Schlemihl a byword for the luckless man. Shadowless, Peter wanders the world learning what men truly prize. The fable still reads freshly.
870-the-love-of-ulrich-nebendahl:
Jerome K. Jerome wrote this tale of Ulrich Nebendahl, a German student whose love troubles the Herr Professor and his circle. The story, published in 1908, follows Ulrich through the hopes and humiliations of first love, in a university town where books and beer mix with romance.

Jerome writes with warmth for young love and with humour for the elders who watch it. His tone is gentle, never mocking, and the tale ends in the bittersweet key of youth. The piece suits readers who enjoy Jerome's softer stories, where a small love affair becomes a picture of a whole world.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-joseph-nirsch:
Joseph Nirschl was a Bavarian theologian who specialized in the Church Fathers. Born at Durchfurth in 1823, he was ordained in 1851, took a theology doctorate at Munich in 1854, and taught Christian doctrine at Passau. In 1862 he became professor of church history and patrology, the study of the Fathers, and in 1879 he moved to Würzburg.

His chief work was a three-volume textbook of patrology and patristics from 1881 to 1885. He also wrote on Augustine's teaching on evil, on the Immaculate Conception, and on St. Ignatius of Antioch, whose letters he translated into German with the catecheses of St. Cyril of Jerusalem. He defended the genuineness of pseudo-Dionysius and King Abgar's letter.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-neusohl:
Neusohl is a diocese in Hungary, founded in 1776 by Maria Theresa. Cardinal Peter Pazmany had already planned four new sees to relieve Gran, including Neusohl, but that project lapsed in 1636. Instead four Jesuit colleges rose at Kassa, Neusohl, Kossy and Safron. After the Jesuit suppression, the diocese project revived.

On 7 December 1775 Maria Theresa told Gran's chapter of the decision and asked what revenues it would assign. Royal decision founded the diocese on 11 January 1776, and the papal decree appeared on 13 March. Baron Franz Berchtold, first bishop from 1776 to 1793, held the first canonical visitation from 1778 to 1785. His material efforts failed, and the great fire of 1782, which destroyed the episcopal residence, so harmed the see that Joseph II considered giving it up. The entry follows its bishops, seminary, lyceum and archdeaneries.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-nikolaus-von-:
Vienna theologian Nikolaus von Dinkelsbühl, born around 1360, led his university and spoke for Austria at Constance. A master by 1390, he taught philosophy, mathematics, and physics, served as dean and rector, and took his theology doctorate in 1409.

Canon of Saint Stephen's from 1405, he acted as ambassador for university and prince, represented Duke Albert V at the Council of Constance, and preached on ending the schism. His sermons and theological writings circulated widely, and he died at Mariazell in 1433. He declined re-election as rector in 1409, though he had served the university in 1405.
chamisso-peter-schlemihl:
A man sells his shadow to a gray stranger for a purse that never empties, and learns what the bargain costs. Adelbert von Chamisso's Peter Schlemihl, from 1814, appears here in English translation. Without a shadow, Peter finds every door in society quietly closed to him.

The tale reads like a fairy story and aches like a confession. Wealth without belonging turns to ashes in his hands, and love slips beyond his reach. Chamisso, himself a French-born exile in Germany, knew the outsider's position from inside. The classic fable of selling one's soul for gold gains unusual melancholy in his telling. It remains one of the great short works of German Romanticism.

tea-cup-reading-and-fortune-telling-by-t: Tea-Cup Reading and Fortune-Telling by Tea Leaves is by a Highland Seer. George Sully and Company of New York issued the book. Ten plates of cups support the text. The parts first set out the roots of the art. They then give the rite and method of using the cup. Broad rules for reading the cup come next. A long A-to-Z list of signs gives their meanings. Sample cups are then worked out in full. A part on omens closes the book.
the-love-of-ulrich-nebendahl:
Jerome K. Jerome's The Love of Ulrich Nebendahl was published in New York by Dodd, Mead and Company in 1909, from a 1904 copyright. The story opens in a Saxon village, where the pastor, Herr Pfarrer Winckelmann, is troubled most of all by Ulrich's bachelor state. As father of the village, he feels bound to see his children marry well, and he urges Ulrich that keeping the hearth fire alive is a citizen's duty.

Over beer, the pastor recalls that at Ulrich's age he already had two boys and a girl. Ulrich answers dreamily that his heart always goes out to the little ones. The pastor then names a candidate: Elsa, good, pious, and economical, whose price is above rubies. Ulrich's face lights at her name, and Jerome lets a matchmaking talk carry the romance's start.
the-national-preacher-vol-2-no-6-nov-182:
Volume 2, No. 6 of The National Preacher, dated November 1827, is present here only as a sermon heading, title page, and subscription notices, so the sermon itself does not appear. Sermon XXV, by the Rev. Mr. Patton, heads the number. The magazine's subtitle promises original monthly sermons from living ministers, edited by the Rev. Austin Dickinson of New York.

A special notice tells subscribers in city and country to send payments to the editor or a named agent, adding that candid men need not be told twice. Postage is stated at one and a half cents under a hundred miles and two and a half cents beyond. J. and J. Harper printed the number at 82 Cliff Street, New York.
the-national-preacher-vol-2-no-7-dec-182:
Volume 2, No. 7 of The National Preacher, dated December 1827, is present here only as title matter and a publisher's proposal, so its two sermons do not appear. Sermons XXVI, by the Rev. Dr. Leland, and XXVII, by the Rev. Mr. Baldwin, are named at the head. The magazine, edited by the Rev. Austin Dickinson in New York, printed original monthly sermons from living ministers.

Most of the pages shown propose a new periodical, The American Pastor's Journal, to be filled with sketches of real characters and striking facts furnished chiefly by clergymen. Its fourteen planned topics range from instances of very early piety and cases of conviction to death-bed scenes of Christians, backsliders, and infidels.
